disclaimer: All people, instruments, prices, rates and events are fictional and synthetic. They illustrate ideas from the lessons. They don't predict real returns and are not product recommendations.

instruments.name: Easy Access Savings
instruments.description: Safe and available any day at no cost. Grows slowly and can trail inflation.

instruments.name: Locked Deposit 1 year
instruments.description: Fixed interest for 12 months. Taking money out early loses the interest earned plus 1% of the amount. Stops growing at maturity.

instruments.name: Locked Deposit 2 years
instruments.description: Fixed interest for 24 months. Taking money out early loses the interest earned plus 1% of the amount. Stops growing at maturity.

instruments.name: Locked Deposit 3 years
instruments.description: Fixed interest for 36 months. Taking money out early loses the interest earned plus 1% of the amount. Stops growing at maturity.

instruments.name: Locked Deposit 5 years
instruments.description: Fixed interest for 60 months. Taking money out early loses the interest earned plus 1% of the amount. Stops growing at maturity.

instruments.name: Steady State Bond Fund
instruments.description: A fund of stable government bonds. Steady, but the price can dip, for example when interest rates rise.

instruments.name: Rocket Corp High-Yield Fund
instruments.description: Bonds of weaker companies. Higher interest makes up for credit risk: some borrowers may not pay back.

instruments.name: World Market Basket
instruments.description: A low-cost index basket of companies from around the world. Diversified, but it still falls when the whole market falls.

instruments.name: Premium Star Active Fund
instruments.description: An actively managed fund that aims to beat the market. Charges a much higher yearly fee.

instruments.name: Tech Leaders Basket
instruments.description: A basket of technology companies only. Many holdings, but one theme, so less diversified than it looks.

instruments.name: Nova Robotics
instruments.description: A single fictional robotics company. Can grow fast or lose much of its value.

instruments.name: Helio Foods
instruments.description: A single fictional food company. Steadier than most single stocks, still concentrated.

instruments.name: HypeCoin
instruments.description: A fictional trending token with no underlying income. Its price is driven by mood and hype.

instruments.name: HypeCoin 2× Leveraged
instruments.description: HypeCoin bought with borrowed money: gains and losses are doubled. It is worth 0 for good once it falls 50% from the start.

instruments.name: Retirement Account: World Basket
instruments.description: The World Market Basket inside a retirement account. Growth is tax-free if the money stays until the end; taking it out early costs 10% plus the tax.

instruments.name: Retirement Account: Bond Mix
instruments.description: Government bonds inside a retirement account. Tax-free growth if the money stays until the end; taking it out early costs 10% plus the tax.

scenarios.title: Kuba's Safety Cushion

persona.name: Kuba
persona.situation: First job on a 6-month contract that may not be renewed. No savings cushion yet.

scenarios.goal: Pay the car repair without a loss and still have a cushion at the end.

traps.label: All in the basket
traps.why: The repair may have to be paid by selling a falling basket.

traps.label: Long lock-up
traps.why: The repair triggers the early-withdrawal penalty, and the rest stays locked.

debriefPoints: An emergency fund needs liquidity first.
One year is too short to recover from a drop.
Here a forced sale is a bigger risk than inflation.

scenarios.title: Lena and Tom's Wedding

persona.name: Lena and Tom
persona.situation: Wedding booked for a fixed date in 2 years. The venue is paid on that day.

scenarios.goal: Have the full wedding budget on the day.

traps.label: Higher rate, wrong term
traps.why: It matures after the wedding, so the money comes out early with a penalty.

traps.label: Chasing interest
traps.why: Credit risk: the fund's price can be down on the wedding day.

debriefPoints: Match the term to the date you need the money.
A higher rate usually means a riskier borrower or less access.

scenarios.title: Marek's Favourite Company

persona.name: Marek
persona.situation: Engineer with a stable job and an emergency fund already in place. A big fan of Nova Robotics who wants to go all in.

traps.label: All in
traps.why: One company's problems hit the whole portfolio.

traps.label: One theme
traps.why: Looks spread out, but everything depends on the same industry.

debriefPoints: A single stock carries the full damage of one company's problems.
A narrow basket is less diversified than it looks.
A stock fits as a small part of a long-term mix.

scenarios.title: Zofia and the Premium Fund

persona.name: Zofia
persona.situation: Inherited money. An adviser recommends the Premium Star active fund with glossy marketing.

scenarios.goal: Grow the inheritance for later life.

traps.label: The premium fund
traps.why: Same market as the basket, about 1.6% a year more in fees.

traps.label: Keep it in savings
traps.why: Inflation eats the value over 20 years.

debriefPoints: Fees are charged every year and compound against you.
The active fund moves like the basket but keeps less of the growth.
Ask what the extra cost actually buys.

scenarios.title: Olek's Group-Chat Tip

persona.name: Olek
persona.situation: Student with savings from a summer job. A group chat says HypeCoin can't lose and will 10x by spring. Next semester's tuition comes out of this money.

scenarios.goal: Pay the tuition and keep the rest.

traps.label: Trust the chat
traps.why: The tuition is due after the crash.

traps.label: Double the bet
traps.why: Leverage doubles losses; the position can be wiped out.

debriefPoints: Speculation is a bet on price, not a plan built on value.
Never speculate with money you need soon.
Leverage multiplies losses as well as gains.
Hype peaks before the crash, and late buyers lose the most.

scenarios.title: Nina's Home Deposit

persona.name: Nina
persona.situation: Renting, steady job, emergency fund in place. Plans to buy a flat in 5 years.

scenarios.goal: Have the home deposit ready in 5 years.

traps.label: Only savings
traps.why: Too little growth to reach the target.

traps.label: Only the basket
traps.why: A drop just before the purchase can push it below the floor.

debriefPoints: A medium horizon needs a balance of growth and safety.
Ask the five questions for each pick: risk, return, liquidity, cost and horizon.

scenarios.title: Paula's Uneven Income

persona.name: Paula
persona.situation: Single parent and freelance designer with irregular income. Saving for a child's school costs.

scenarios.goal: A school fund that survives a bad year.

moneyNeeds.label: Two quiet months with no clients

traps.label: 7 years is long
traps.why: The income gap can force a sale during a drop.

traps.label: Lock it all
traps.why: The day-900 need breaks the deposit with a penalty.

debriefPoints: Age and horizon aren't the whole picture.
Unstable income and dependents lower risk capacity.

scenarios.title: Ewa's First Salary

persona.name: Ewa
persona.situation: First full-time job, no expensive debt, emergency fund already built. Investing the first savings for retirement.

scenarios.goal: Grow as much as possible for retirement.

traps.label: Play it safe
traps.why: Loses about a quarter of its real value over 30 years.

traps.label: Pay for a manager
traps.why: The fee drag compounds for 30 years.

debriefPoints: A long horizon and future income allow a growth-oriented mix.
The crash in year 3 has decades to recover.
Starting early is the biggest advantage.

scenarios.title: Sam's University Fund

persona.name: Sam
persona.situation: Steady income and two children. Saving for the eldest's university.

scenarios.goal: Have the university fund ready when the eldest starts.

traps.label: Two favourite stocks
traps.why: Concentrated: two companies decide the child's education.

traps.label: Lock and forget
traps.why: Stops growing after year 5 and stays flat for 10 years.

debriefPoints: Each goal gets its own horizon and mix.
A small cash part covers surprises so the investments can stay put.

scenarios.title: Danuta's Glide Path

persona.name: Danuta
persona.situation: Savings at their largest, plans to retire at 67. Has been 100% in the market basket for 20 years.

scenarios.goal: Protect what's been built and keep growing with inflation.

traps.label: It worked so far
traps.why: The crash at 65 hits the largest balance just before retirement.

traps.label: All to cash
traps.why: Inflation over 12 years, with retirement still ahead.

debriefPoints: Shift from growing to protecting gradually.
Even near retirement, part of the money stays invested for growth.

scenarios.title: Henryk Retires Next Year

persona.name: Henryk
persona.situation: Retires in a year and will live on these savings for the first years of retirement.

scenarios.goal: Fund both years of spending and keep the rest for later retirement.

traps.label: Stay fully invested
traps.why: Both withdrawals are paid by selling after the crash.

traps.label: Lock it all
traps.why: The day-365 withdrawal pays the early-withdrawal penalty.

debriefPoints: Sequence risk: the same drop hurts more when withdrawals start.
A cash buffer of 1-3 years of spending avoids selling at the bottom.

scenarios.title: Ola Minds the Gap

persona.name: Ola
persona.situation: Expects a public pension of 1,800 a month against 3,000 needed: a gap of about 288,000 over 20 years of retirement. Has no separate emergency fund.

scenarios.goal: Close as much of the retirement gap as possible.

traps.label: Everything in the pension
traps.why: The emergency breaks the account: penalty plus tax.

traps.label: Only savings
traps.why: The gap barely moves.

debriefPoints: Tax advantages come with lock-up rules.
The emergency fund stays outside the pension account.
Time and compounding shrink the gap.
